props.title: The Magic Christian

sections.content: The Magic Christian (1969) stands as one of the most acidic satires of capitalism and human greed ever committed to film. Starring Peter Sellers and Ringo Starr, this bizarre British comedy follows eccentric millionaire Guy Grand as he conducts increasingly outrageous social experiments to prove everyone has their price. The film shares DNA with other counterculture classics like Head (1968) and If.... (1968), mercilessly mocking societal institutions through surreal set-pieces. Director Joseph McGrath channels the anarchic spirit of Richard Lester's A Hard Day's Night (1964), but with a much darker edge.

sections.content: The film's development was notably chaotic, with multiple writers including Terry Southern (who wrote the source novel), John Cleese, Graham Chapman, and Peter Sellers himself contributing to the screenplay. This resulted in a fractured, episodic structure similar to Southern's work on Easy Rider (1969) and Dr. Strangelove (1964). The movie's influence can be seen in later works like Brewster McCloud (1970) and MASH (1970), which similarly used dark humor to challenge institutional power. SUBHEAD: Counterculture Cinema and Social Satire

The Magic Christian embodies late 1960s counterculture cinema's rejection of materialist values. Like Performance (1970) and The Ruling Class (1972), it uses the British upper class as a vehicle for broader social criticism. The film's famous climactic scene - where businessmen dive into a vat of excrement and blood for money - remains one of cinema's most memorable metaphors for capitalism. This influenced later anti-establishment films like Brazil (1985) and They Live (1988).
